name: PT Mitra International Resources Tbk

frontmatter.title: A shrinking cement hauler whose assets are in the price and whose earnings are not
frontmatter.summary: Mitra International Resources hauls bag cement on a fleet that shrank again. On the audited operating lines the group loses money at the operating line, and the property sale that repaired the balance sheet does not repeat. The asset value is broadly in the share price; the earnings value is far below it. We stay at REDUCE with a target of Rp15, a single base-case value rather than a probability-weighted blend.
thesis: The operating loss is real and audited, with total operating expenses of 11.5 against gross profit of 7.4 in FY2025A, and an operating loss in every year of the history we model.
Our FY2026E operating loss of -3.6 is the company's own budgeted loss, not a cautious variant of it, so there is no earnings base for a going-concern multiple.
The fleet and property carry real value, and the asset leg of our valuation is Rp22 against an earnings leg of Rp4, so the price sits between them.
The strategic acquisition that drove the promotional move in the shares is a genuine upside path, but with no counterparty, price or timetable it belongs in a one-in-four bull case, not the base.
We stay at REDUCE with a target of Rp15, -23.0% against the price, and we publish the range the evidence supports rather than a single point.

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited accounts, and whether the nine-month gross margin holds through the seasonally weak fourth quarter
Fourth-quarter national cement volume data and disbursement pace of the housing programme
Use of land-sale proceeds, completion of debt repayments and any new fleet capex

blocks.text: We stay at **REDUCE** on Mitra International Resources with a twelve-month target of **Rp15** against a price of Rp19, an expected total return of -23.0%. This is a revision after the first red-team round, and the work changed the numbers in both directions: we restated the audited operating lines, which lifts the earnings value, and we replaced a hand-picked peer median with the house comparables, which cuts it. The net effect is a lower target than the initiation and a less extreme call than the initiation implied.

The company hauls bagged cement for the cement majors on a fleet that has shrunk to 198 trucks trucks from two hundred and eighteen a year earlier [S2]. It is a volume business with a fixed cost base, and the volume has been falling: revenue ran from 84.4 in FY2022A to 63.3 in FY2025A, and the group lost money at the operating line in every year of that history [S4]. On the audited numbers the FY2025A operating loss was -4.1 on operating expenses of 11.5, and depreciation of 9.3 IDR bn is the largest single charge in the cost base [S4].

The balance sheet, not the income statement, is where the value is. Net fixed assets were 157 IDR bn at the end of FY2025A and 115 IDR bn at the end of September 2026, after the group sold its Bogor land and buildings for 55.0 IDR bn [S4][S5]. That sale produced a 16.0 IDR bn accounting gain, repaid bank debt and cut borrowings to 15.9 IDR bn against cash of 0.9 IDR bn [S3][S5]. The sale is why the reported FY2026 result is positive at all, and it is why the equity is not worthless; it is also why the earnings-based value and the asset-based value diverge as far as they do.

Our valuation therefore runs two live legs rather than one. The earnings leg, an EV/EBITDA multiple on the house comparables, is worth Rp4 per share; the asset leg, a P/BV multiple on the peer set the house uses for asset-backed transport names, is worth Rp22. The price of Rp19 sits between them, closer to the asset value. The blended target of Rp15 is below the price because the earnings leg is worth so little, and the call is REDUCE rather than SELL because the asset leg is not. That target is a single base-case value, not a probability-weighted blend: both live legs are struck on trailing EBITDA and current book value, so the bear and bull runs produce the same per-share number, and the risk section shows the operating lines that do differ.

What would change the view, in either direction, is a corporate event rather than a trading quarter. The press attributed the promotional move in the shares to a possible strategic acquisition of the company [S6]; for a business whose tangible assets are several times its market value, a buyer at or near book would validate the top of our range. We carry that path in the bull case with a stated probability and we do not put it in the target, because no counterparty, price or timetable is disclosed [S6][S3].

MIRA provides land transportation services, overwhelmingly the haulage of bagged cement from cement plants and terminals to distributors and project sites, plus a smaller bottled-water haulage book. Its named customers are the cement producers Semen Tiga Roda, Semen Garuda, Semen Bima and Readymix Dynamix, contracted on multi-year terms, and management describes the marketing strategy as concentrating service on cement manufacturers and bottled-water producers that sign cooperation contracts [S2]. Transportation is effectively the whole company: net revenues were 63.3 in FY2025A, the great majority from the transport segment, with the remaining subsidiaries in bodywork, warehousing and oilfield services now described in the annual report as having ceased operations or no longer operating [S2][S4].

The asset base is the business. At the end of FY2025A the group operated 198 trucks trucks, down from two hundred and eighteen a year earlier, and employed 347 people people including drivers [S2]. Net fixed assets stood at 157 IDR bn at that date [S4]. The group then sold its Bogor land and buildings to PT Amanah Gudang Persada for 55.0 IDR bn, signed on the last day of July 2026, at a price equal to a large share of the group's equity, and net fixed assets fell to 115 IDR bn by the end of September [S3][S5]. What remains is a fleet, workshops and depots with limited freehold property.

Strategically the company is doing the only two things available to a sub-scale hauler with a stretched balance sheet: it is selling surplus property to repay bank debt, and it is running a cost efficiency programme while holding on to its cement contracts. The nine months to September 2026 show revenue of 46.0 IDR bn, an operating loss of -1.0 IDR bn before the property gain, and a 16.0 IDR bn gain on the disposal, with bank debt down to 15.9 IDR bn and cash of 0.9 IDR bn [S5]. The company's plan for the year projected revenue of 64.0 IDR bn and still budgeted an operating loss, which is an unusually candid admission that the cost base exceeds the revenue the contracts can generate [S2].

In the competitive hierarchy MIRA is a challenger, not a leader. The Indonesian cement haulage market is fragmented across owner-driver fleets and the logistics arms of the cement producers themselves; MIRA's distinguishing asset is its long-standing contracts with the majors rather than scale, technology or price leadership [S2]. Its footprint follows the cement plants and distribution network, concentrated on Java, and its revenue is therefore levered to Java bag-cement volumes and to the housing and infrastructure pipeline rather than to national aggregates [S2][S7].

Cement haulage economics are unkind to small operators. A truck earns a tariff per tonne moved and
per kilometre travelled, while the cost base is dominated by diesel, tyres, maintenance and driver
wages, most of which are fixed once the truck is bought and depreciated on a schedule that does not
flex with utilisation. When cement demand softens, the producer spreads the same tonnage over its
preferred carriers, utilisation falls, and the carrier absorbs the fixed cost. Scale helps because
it spreads depot, workshop and administrative overhead; contract length helps because it protects
tariffs; and modern trucks help because fuel and repair cost per tonne are lower. A carrier that
cannot reinvest in its fleet slowly loses both the efficiency and the contract, which is the loop
this company is trying to break.

The demand side is cement, and cement is in a slow recovery from a weak base. The largest Indonesian producer reported domestic cement sales volume growing 4.2% in the nine months to September 2026, with bagged cement up 4.6% and bulk growing more slowly, and the same disclosure repeats the structural problem of overcapacity and rising energy costs [S7]. MIRA's annual report describes national bag-cement sales as stagnant through 2025, with the company's revenue falling for that reason rather than through loss of a specific contract [S2]. The two statements are consistent once the years are separated: 2025 was flat, and the first nine months of 2026 show a modest recovery that is strongest in the bagged segment where MIRA operates. The initiation understated that recovery by misreading the producer's volume disclosure, and we correct it here.

The policy driver we watch is housing. The government's programme to build three million houses is named by both the cement producer and by MIRA as the main potential catalyst for bag-cement demand, and the producer links it, alongside infrastructure and data-centre construction, to the volume growth it has already reported [S2][S7]. We take the programme seriously as a demand support but not as a tariff event: it raises tonnes moved, and only indirectly the price per tonne, and MIRA's ability to capture the tonnes is limited by fleet capacity that has been shrinking [S2][S4].

Competitive intensity is high and the moat is thin. There are no switching costs of consequence for a cement producer allocating tonnage across hauliers, no network effect, no proprietary technology and no brand premium in a commodity service; the only durable advantages are contract tenure, depot proximity to the plants and a fleet in good condition [S2]. MIRA has the first, is losing the third, and its bargaining position with customers is weak enough that management states tariffs could not be increased in a year of rising costs [S2]. On the five-forces view, supplier power (diesel, tyres, truck OEMs) is high, buyer power is high and concentrated in a handful of cement majors, the threat of new owner-driver capacity is high, substitutes are limited to rail and bulk handling, and rivalry is intense among sub-scale carriers chasing flat volumes.

Regulation touches the business in three places: the housing programme and infrastructure budget as demand drivers; fuel pricing, because diesel is the largest variable cost and the subsidised price is a policy variable; and the road-transport regime, including axle-load enforcement that determines how much cement a truck may legally carry [S2][S7]. None of these is within the company control, and none is currently moving in its favour strongly enough to change the tariff picture management describes.

In commodity haulage the winning operator is the low-cost one, not the best-connected one. Cost per
tonne-kilometre is driven by fleet age, route density, backhaul utilisation and driver productivity,
and the operators that compound value are those that reinvest on schedule and keep contract
tenure with the producers. Sub-scale carriers with ageing fleets tend to trade at a discount to
book because the market prices the replacement capex they have deferred.

The reported history is a slow contraction. Revenue fell from 84.4 in FY2022A to 77.2, 66.0 and 63.3 in FY2025A, with the latest decline of -4.2% attributed by management to stagnant national cement sales, an older and smaller fleet, and tariffs that could not be raised [S2][S4]. Operating profit was negative in every year of that history, from -25.6 to -4.1, and the group has run a retained deficit that leaves equity at 145.9 against a share count of 3,961 m shares [S4][S5].

Depreciation is the line on which the reported numbers mislead. The data pack carries a depreciation charge that is only the administrative slice of the real figure; the audited notes show a total charge of 9.3 IDR bn in FY2025A and 9.7 IDR bn in FY2024A, most of it inside cost of revenues [S4]. We restate both years, which turns the pack's negative EBITDA into 5.1 and makes the operating loss the honest measure of the business. Interest is the second quiet killer: 4.3 of finance cost against an operating loss produced a net loss to owners of -8.2 [S4].

Two lines in the pack are not the audited ones, and the second of them is the operating expense line. The pack's operating expenses sit roughly a tenth above the filing; the audited accounts show total operating expenses of 11.5 and an operating loss of -4.1 [S4]. We restate both, which raises restated FY2025A EBITDA to 5.1 rather than the lower figure the initiation used, and every FY2026E cost line follows from that base. The depreciation rate itself is set by asset lives rather than by a claim about the fleet's age: the group depreciates trucks over four to eight years, buildings over fifteen to twenty and land not at all [S4], so the charge tracks the depreciable base, which fell with the disposal from 157 IDR bn to 115 IDR bn [S5]. Applying the same ratio gives the forward run-rate we carry, 6.7 in FY2026E. The initiation's basis said the fleet was near the end of its depreciable life; the disclosed lives do not support that and we withdraw it.

The nine months to September 2026 change the balance sheet, not the business. Revenue of 46.0 IDR bn and an operating loss of -1.0 IDR bn before the disposal show the same economics; the 16.0 IDR bn gain on the Bogor property turns the reported result positive, and the proceeds cut bank debt to 15.9 IDR bn with cash of 0.9 IDR bn [S5]. Equity attributable to owners was 145.9 at the FY2025 year-end and 161 IDR bn at the end of September, the difference being the disposal gain and the quarter's result [S4][S5]. Minority interests are negative -6.5 IDR bn, because the dormant transport and oilfield-service subsidiaries have accumulated deficits; that is a real feature of the equity, not a rounding item, and we use the interim figure throughout rather than the pack's older one [S5]. Working capital is small for a hauler, 3.7 in FY2025A, because the cement majors pay on contract terms and there is no inventory [S4].

Our forecast follows the company's revenue plan of 64.0 IDR bn for FY2026E, which is 64.0 in the model, then nominal growth of a few per cent a year as bag-cement volumes recover modestly while fleet capacity caps what MIRA can carry [S2][S7]. The cost lines are the point of the revision. Operating expenses of 12.9 are not a haircut from the last actual but the level the company's own projection implies: on our gross margin, the company's budgeted operating loss is reproduced by the expense ratio we carry, which is why our FY2026E operating loss of -3.6 is the company's own number and not a cautious variant of it [S2]. We withdraw the initiation's claim that costs stay at the last actual in real terms, which the company's own budget contradicts [S2]. Gross margin is held at 14.5%, in line with the nine-month run-rate once the sold property's running costs drop out [S5], and EBITDA margin falls from 8.1% in FY2025A to 4.9% because the revenue plan does not cover the cost base. The result is EBITDA of 3.1 but EBIT of -3.6, because depreciation of 6.7 on a fleet that must be replaced exceeds the margin the contracts generate.

Capacity and capex have to be read together. The revenue path assumes no fleet growth at all: the 198 trucks trucks stay 198 trucks, and the nominal growth is tariff and price inflation on the same tonnage, not new capacity [S2]. Capex of 5.8 in FY2026E and around the same share of revenue thereafter is replacement of a shrinking fleet, not expansion, which is why revenue can grow in nominal terms without new units. The initiation implied growth needed capacity it did not fund; the resolution is that there is no volume growth in the path, and the fleet constraint is a cap on upside rather than a contradiction in the base case [S2][S4].

Cash flow is the binding constraint, and the balance sheet needs care. Capex of 7.6 in FY2025A was already close to operating cash generation, and our base case produces free cash flow of -2.4 in FY2026E and negative free cash flow in every year after it [S4][S5]. Net debt on the model path is 29.3 at the FY2026E year-end and 51.6 by FY2030E, or 13.0 EBITDA. That path is not the actual balance sheet: the corporate model has no asset-disposal line, so it books the accounting gain and the debt repayment but not the cash receipt, and its forecast cash line is therefore negative from FY2026E while its debt line of 17.7 is close to the filed figure. We say plainly that the model's cash line is an artefact of the missing disposal and not a forecast of insolvency, and every leverage and multiple statement in this report uses the actual September balance sheet - bank debt of 15.9 IDR bn against cash of 0.9 IDR bn, under three times restated trailing EBITDA - rather than the model path [S3][S5].

That funding gap is the central financial risk and we do not model it away. The group has no disclosed facility, no announced rights issue and no dividend, and the proceeds of the only disposal it had are spent. If free cash flow stays negative, the next fleet renewal is funded by debt or by another asset sale, and we carry that in the bear case rather than assuming a recapitalisation the filings do not describe [S3][S5].

Capital allocation is defensively sound but value-neutral: sell property, repay the most expensive debt, defer fleet renewal. That preserves solvency and destroys the earnings base, because a hauler that does not renew trucks loses the tonnage that pays for them. Dividends are zero and the payout ratio is 0.0; with a retained deficit and a just-restructured banking relationship, we do not expect a distribution in the forecast period [S0][S5].

Earnings quality is taken in full in the governance section. In summary, the accruals position is not the problem: cash flow from operations exceeded the net result in each of the last three fiscal years, and the negative accruals ratio reflects the depreciation charge rather than aggressive revenue recognition [S0]. The problems are the fourth-quarter true-up, the reliance of the reported result on a disposal gain, and the negative minority interest, all of which we treat as optics-class rather than manipulation-class flags [S4][S5].

The method set is weighted toward the asset and multiple view rather than the cash flow, and the weights changed in this revision. MIRA is capital-intensive, loss-making and has negative free cash flow in every forecast year, so the discounted cash flow floors the equity at zero and returns nothing at any discount rate. That is a finding about the going concern, not a valuation input, and the initiation's four tenths of weight on it was mechanically cutting the target by two fifths for no reason. We cut it to 10%, keep EV/EBITDA at 30% for the operating recovery a trade buyer would underwrite, and put 60% on P/BV because the fleet and property are the value and the house values the comparable transport names on book. P/E is dropped because the group is loss-making [S4][S5].

The cost of capital build follows the house convention: the rupiah risk-free rate, the mature-market equity premium plus the Indonesia country premium, an industry unlevered beta relevered for the modest net debt, and a pre-tax cost of debt in the high single digits taken from the restated Bank Mestika Dharma facilities disclosed in the interim accounts [S5]. That produces a cost of equity of 12.8% and a weighted average cost of capital of 11.9%, inside the house band for rupiah names and appropriate for a small, illiquid, loss-making industrial.

The DCF is the honest but unhelpful leg. With EBIT below the depreciation charge, free cash flow is negative through the forecast, and the enterprise value the model produces is -40.5, which after net debt and minorities floors the equity at Rp0. The terminal value is 44.8% of a negative gross present value, which is a negative perpetuity rather than a terminal state; we report it because it is what the model produces, and we give it a residual weight precisely because it cannot discriminate between values [S4][S5].

The EV/EBITDA leg is the operating view and its peer basis was wrong in the initiation. That version used twelve names and a trailing multiple that did not reconcile to the house comparables: the same companies carried multiples roughly double to triple the house figures, and the resulting median of about eight times was not the house peer median at all. We now use the four house-covered Indonesian transport names that own assets of the kind MIRA owns - BIRD, SMDR, TAXI and WEHA - and we state the basis rather than implying a reconciliation. The leg applies their trailing EV/EBITDA, median 4.9 on three names (TAXI carries no EBITDA line), because the metric it multiplies, our trailing EBITDA, is measured over the same trailing period. That median is not their house current-year multiple and must not be read as one: the same three names on the house FY2026E basis carry multiples of a third to a half of their trailing figures, a median of about two and a quarter times, and at that same-peer current-year multiple the leg collapses from Rp4 to roughly a quarter of itself [S0]. The published 4.9 sits next to the sixteen-name house current-year median, but that is a cross-set, cross-period coincidence and we do not present it as a reconciliation any more. We keep the trailing basis because the leg's own metric is trailing and because it is the basis every other house multiple in this note is struck on; a reader who prefers the current-year basis should read the leg as approximately nil, which is the direction the financial section already points to with its operating loss. Applied to restated trailing EBITDA and after the restated net debt and negative minorities, the trailing basis gives Rp4 per share [S0][S4]. The wider peer list also carries one cement-bag converter whose multiple reflects packaging margins rather than haulage; including it would lift the median and move the target above the price, and we exclude it on the business ground that it is not a carrier, stating the sensitivity rather than hiding it [S0].

The asset leg is the one the initiation was missing. MIRA's value is a fleet of 198 trucks trucks, workshops and depots, and the Bogor sale cleared at a premium to its book value, so book value is a floor rather than a ceiling on what the assets can realise [S3][S5]. The four transport peers the house values on book carry a median P/BV of 0.5, which on restated parent equity of 161 IDR bn gives Rp22 per share. That is the leg that reconciles the apparent contradiction the red team identified: at the initiation's target the market was paying a fraction of net book for a company whose property had just sold above book, and no source justified that impairment [S3][S5].

The two legs bracket the price. Earnings value is Rp4, asset value is Rp22, the blend is Rp14, and after the house liquidity discount of 0.1 for a stock with three-month traded value of 696,422,434.9 the target is Rp15 [S0]. We publish that range rather than a point estimate because the evidence does not carry a point: the earnings leg assumes the cost base never earns its cost of capital, the asset leg assumes a buyer pays peer book for the fleet, and the truth for a minority holder is between them. The rating is set on the blend, and it is REDUCE rather than SELL because the asset leg is not a theoretical construct - it is what the last disposal realised [S3].

The blend is a weight argument, and we publish the cliff rather than let the reader find it. At half P/BV, two fifths EV/EBITDA and a residual tenth on the floored DCF, the same two legs in those proportions give a blend of about thirteen rupiah after the forward roll and the liquidity discount, an expected return near minus a third, and SELL rather than REDUCE. At the industry default weights the model would carry on a name like this - three fifths DCF floored at zero, a quarter EV/EBITDA and the remainder on P/E, the last unavailable because the group is loss-making - the target is the earnings leg alone, around one rupiah, and the call is unambiguously SELL. Both figures are published here because they are the honest frame: the REDUCE depends entirely on the three-fifths asset weight, and a reader who rejects that weight should treat the name as a SELL. We keep the weight, and we argue it from the evidence rather than from a preference: the last disposal cleared above net book value, the peer book multiples the leg uses are the same four names the house covers, and there is no sourced impairment that would justify marking the fleet below book [S3][S5][S0]. What we do not claim is that the weight is neutral - it is the single assumption that keeps the call out of SELL.

Sensitivity is dominated by the multiple and the margin, not by the discount rate. Because the DCF is floored at zero, moving WACC by a percentage point changes nothing; what moves the target is the EBITDA the fleet generates and the multiple the market applies to it [S4][S5].

What the price implies is the crux. At Rp19 the shares trade on 31.3x EV/EBITDA and 0.5x book. The book multiple is not evidence of overvaluation - it is a value signal, and the asset leg says so; the initiation used it as corroboration and that was a mistake. The overvaluation case rests entirely on the earnings multiple: to justify the price on the earnings leg, EBITDA would have to rise several-fold from a base that is barely positive after the full depreciation charge, with no capex to support the fleet that would carry such volumes [S2][S4]. Put differently, the market is paying for the assets and a recovery in tariffs at the same time, and only the assets are evidenced.

Two structure points complete the valuation. The authorised capital is three times the issued shares, not double as the initiation said, so the dilution headroom is larger than we represented; the relevant figures are the authorised twelve billion shares against the 3,961 m shares issued [S4]. And the liquidity discount is the house schedule applied to the traded value, not an analyst judgement: 696,422,434.9 of three-month traded value sits in the band that carries a 0.1 discount, and we have not overridden it [S0].

The downside risks we weight most heavily are operational and financial rather than cyclical. The first is liquidity and funding: before the land sale the group had overdue salaries and other payables and was restructuring bank facilities, and the proceeds repaid long-term and short-term debt rather than funding the business [S3][S5]. The sale has bought time, not solvency, free cash flow is negative in every year of our forecast, and the next maturity wall arrives with a fleet that still needs replacing - likelihood medium, impact high. The second is customer concentration: a handful of cement majors set the tariffs, and management states they could not be raised in the latest year despite rising costs, so a single contract renegotiation would remove a large share of revenue [S2] - likelihood medium, impact high.

The third is the fleet: at 198 trucks units and falling, capacity caps the tonnage MIRA can win even if demand recovers, and the capex to reverse it competes with debt service [S2][S4] - likelihood high, impact medium. The fourth is cost: diesel, tyres and driver wages are outside management's control and the company has no pricing power to pass them through [S2] - likelihood high, impact medium. The fifth is the fourth-quarter true-up: the audited fourth quarter of 2025 carried a disproportionate share of the annual operating expense charge, and if that pattern repeats our FY2026E margin is at risk in the quarter the market is least prepared for it [S4] - likelihood medium, impact medium, and it is a scenario shock rather than a footnote.

The sixth is governance and structure: the group has no disclosed controlling shareholder above its two named minority holders, the authorised capital is three times its issued shares, and the stock was the subject of a sharp promotional move with no management statement to explain it [S3][S4][S6] - likelihood medium, impact medium. The seventh is the land-sale gain itself: it is already in reported profit, it does not repeat, and any use of the proceeds other than debt repayment would be a red flag to monitor [S5] - likelihood low, impact high.

Our scenarios shock the same three drivers by mirrored amounts: revenue growth by three percentage points either way, gross margin by one and a half points, and the operating-expense ratio by two points, with probabilities of one quarter bear, one half base and one quarter bull. Those weights are likelihood labels for the operating cases only; they do not weight the target, and the assumptions file says so. The bear case has cement demand rolling over again, tariffs pushed down, diesel and wages up, a heavier fourth-quarter true-up, and the group reaching the end of the disposal proceeds with a renewal bill it cannot fund. The bull case has two documented paths: the operating path, where the housing programme and the bagged-cement recovery lift tonnage at existing tariffs with younger units cutting cost per tonne [S2][S7]; and the corporate-action path, where the strategic acquisition that drove the promotional move is completed at or near asset value [S6]. We give the two paths a combined one-in-four probability and do not put the control premium in the target, because no counterparty, price or timetable is disclosed [S6].

The scenario targets converge, and we state why rather than hide it. The multiple leg is applied to trailing EBITDA and the P/BV leg to restated book, so both are scenario-invariant, and the DCF is floored at zero in every case because free cash flow is negative even in the bull case. The probability weights therefore multiply three identical numbers, and the target is a single-scenario value - the base case - not a probability-weighted one. Doubling the bear probability changes nothing, which is itself the demonstration that the published target does not carry scenario information. The dispersion lives in the underlying lines, revenue, margin and free cash flow, which the table shows, and a reader who wants the spread should read the forecast lines rather than the target row [S4][S5].

What would change our view, and in which direction. Upward: a signed contract renewal with a cement major at a higher tariff, disclosed fleet capex funded from operations, or a credible new controlling shareholder injecting capital. Downward: a lost contract, a failed debt restructuring, or a further asset sale whose proceeds leave the group rather than repay debt. Between updates we watch monthly cement volume data, the quarterly interim accounts, and any disclosure on fleet renewal [S5][S7].

Ownership is dispersed by IDX standards. The share register at the end of September 2026 shows two named holders, Intikencana Pranajati and Mitra Murni Expressindo, each with a minority stake, and the public holding the remainder; the data pack's free float is 82.3% [S3][S5]. There is no disclosed controlling shareholder, which cuts both ways: no related-party gravity of the kind that characterises family-controlled IDX names, but also no anchor investor to recapitalise a loss-making business. A large individual holder exited a significant stake in 2025 before the promotional move in the shares, which we read as a signal about insiders' own view of value [S6].

The board is small and conventional: Beni Prananto as President Commissioner, Huda Nardono as the independent commissioner, Wirawan Halim as President Director, with Darminto and Arda Billy as directors, per the deed recited in the material-transaction disclosure [S3]. The audit is performed by Irfan Waluyo & Rekan, a small registered firm; the FY2025 report carries an unmodified opinion stating that the consolidated statements present fairly, in all material respects, the financial position and performance of the group in accordance with Indonesian Financial Accounting Standards [S4]. We note the auditor's size as a governance consideration rather than a red flag, and we found no going-concern emphasis in the opinion text we could extract.

The house earnings-quality contract, line by line. On accruals, cash flow from operations exceeded the net result in each of the last three fiscal years, so the accruals ratio is negative throughout and there is no persistent earnings-outruns-cash signal; the ratio is negative because depreciation is a large non-cash charge, which is the opposite of a manipulation flag [S0][S4]. On divergence, the receivables balance did not grow faster than revenue over the period and there is no capitalised development or borrowing cost line, so those screens are clean; the one genuine distortion is the fourth-quarter expense true-up in FY2025, which we treat as a classification and timing issue and handle by anchoring the expense ratio on the company's own budget [S4][S5]. On the IDX regime, the house record carries MIRA as a listed main-board name with no special notation, and we found no suspension, special-monitoring or unusual-market-activity notice in the sources we archived after the promotional move; the move itself is documented and unexplained by management, which is a flag we report rather than resolve [S0][S6].

On related parties, the LK discloses related-party receivables and payables but no related-party revenue in the segment note, so there is no related-party share of revenue to report; the Bogor sale was disclosed as a material transaction with an unrelated buyer, and the announcement recites the share register precisely because the test is control [S3][S4][S5]. On structure, we found no pledge disclosure over the named holdings in the filings we read and flag that absence as unverified rather than clean; the negative minority interest of -6.5 IDR bn is a real structural feature; the authorised capital is three times the issued shares, which is dilution headroom and not a manipulation flag; and the FY2025 accounts carry fixed assets at cost less depreciation under PSAK 16, with no revaluation surplus, so book value is not inflated by a revaluation exercise [S4][S5]. The dividend record is empty: no distribution in the price history available to us, consistent with the retained deficit [S0][S5]. Our classification: no manipulation-class flag found, several optics-class flags, and the promotional share price is the one item we cannot explain from the filings.

ESG exposures are operational and specific. The fleet burns diesel, so emissions track tonnes moved and fleet age; older trucks emit and cost more per tonne, which aligns the decarbonisation and the renewal argument. Driver safety and working hours are the material social issues for a hauler employing 347 people people including drivers, and the annual report sustainability section addresses workforce composition rather than safety metrics in the passages we reviewed [S2]. Governance is the weakest pillar: a promotional share price with no management statement, no controlling anchor, and substantial unissued capital available for dilution [S3][S6].

The dated catalysts are the reporting calendar and the demand data. The FY2026 audited accounts, expected in March 2027, will show whether the nine-month gross margin survives the seasonally weak fourth quarter and whether the disposal gain is the only reason the year is profitable [S5]. National cement volume data, published monthly and quarterly by the producers, tell us within weeks whether the bag-cement recovery is holding; the largest producer's nine-month volume growth of 4.2% and its bagged segment growth of 4.6% are the base we carry [S7]. On the balance sheet, completion of the debt repayments from the sale proceeds and any announcement of fleet capex are the two disclosures that would move our view [S3][S5].

The KPIs we monitor between updates are: tonnes hauled and revenue per truck (the only honest measure of utilisation, currently only inferable from revenue and fleet count); fleet units, which have fallen to 198 trucks; gross margin, at 14.5% in our base case; operating profit before disposal gains, at -3.6; free cash flow of -2.4; and the actual balance-sheet position of 15.9 IDR bn of bank debt against 0.9 IDR bn of cash [S2][S5]. We also watch the share register for any new holder crossing a disclosure threshold, because a strategic buyer of the fleet is the one path to value above our target that does not require the cement contracts to re-price [S3].

S0.title: Yahoo Finance statements, prices and profile for MIRA.JK

S6.title: Saham MIRA Melonjak 675%, Dipicu Sentimen Akuisisi

bear.narrative: Cement demand rolls over again and the cement majors push haulage tariffs down while diesel and wages rise; with the fleet already at 198 units and no cash to renew it, revenue falls 3pp a year faster than base and gross margin gives up 1.5pp as fixed depot costs are spread over fewer tonnes. The fourth-quarter true-up is heavier than the company's own budget assumed, so operating expenses run two points above our base ratio, and the group reaches the end of the disposal proceeds with a renewal capex bill it cannot fund.

bull.narrative: Two paths, both documented. The operating path: the three-million-house programme and the recovery already visible in bagged cement volumes lift haulage demand, MIRA wins incremental contract tonnage at existing tariffs, revenue runs 3pp a year above base and gross margin is 1.5pp better as younger replacement units cut repair and fuel cost per tonne, with operating expenses two points below base. The corporate-action path: the strategic acquisition that drove the 675% move in the shares is completed at or near asset value, which for a fleet-heavy company is the P/BV leg rather than the earnings leg. We give the two paths a combined one-in-four probability and do not put the control premium in the target, because no counterparty, price or timetable is disclosed.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is the company's own published 2026 projection of Rp 64.0bn against FY2025 revenue of Rp 63.3bn. FY2027E-FY2030E carry +3% nominal: national bag-cement volumes are recovering (+4.2% domestic volume, +4.6% bag cement at SIG in 9M-2026) but MIRA's own fleet is shrinking (218 to 198 units in 2025) and management says tariffs cannot yet be raised, so volume growth is capped by haulage capacity and nominal growth runs close to tariff inflation.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: 14.5%: the nine months to 30 Sep 2026 print 15.3% (revenue Rp 46.0bn less cost of revenues Rp 38.9bn) after 0.5% in the same period of 2025, but the fourth quarter is seasonally the weakest and the 9M figure still carries a full depreciation charge on the disposed Bogor buildings for seven months. Held flat afterwards - no sourced evidence that haulage tariffs rise faster than fuel, wages and tyre costs.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: 20.1% in FY2026E: the company's own 2026 projection budgets an operating loss of Rp 3.584bn on revenue of Rp 64.0bn (S2 p.67), which on our 14.5% gross margin implies operating expenses of about Rp 12.9bn, or 20.1% of revenue. That is consistent with the audited FY2025 ratio of 18.16% and with the fourth-quarter true-up that lifted Q4-2025 operating expenses to 47.6% of Q4 revenue (S4), and it sits above the 17.6% nine-month 2026 ratio (S5) because the fourth quarter is where the annual charge lands. FY2027E-FY2030E ease to 19.0% as the sold site's running costs leave the group, not to the nine-month run-rate.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: 10.5% then 10.0%: depreciation scales with the depreciable base, and net fixed assets fell from Rp 156.7bn at 31 Dec 2025 to Rp 115.3bn at 30 Sep 2026 after the Rp 39.1bn net book value of the Bogor land and buildings left the group (S5). Applying the base ratio to the audited FY2025 charge of Rp 9.28bn gives about Rp 6.8bn, or 10.7% of revenue. The rate follows the disclosed asset lives - trucks over four to eight years, buildings over fifteen to twenty, land not depreciated (S4 p.27) - and not any claim that the fleet is fully depreciated.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: 11%: the fleet is 198 units against 218 a year earlier and management attributes the revenue decline to older, smaller capacity, so replacement is the binding constraint on the business. FY2025 capex was 12.0% of revenue (Rp 7.59bn); nine-month 2026 capex was only Rp 2.24bn because the group was selling assets, which is not a sustainable run-rate for a hauler that must renew trucks.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: 6% of revenue, close to the FY2025 closing ratio of 5.9% and below the FY2024 level of 19.0% that included receivables since collected; cement majors pay on contract terms and the group has no inventory to speak of.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: 10%: the group has run at a loss for four straight years and carries a retained deficit, so cash tax is limited to the final-tax elements already inside operating expenses; 10% is a conservative placeholder for the deferred component rather than a statutory 22% charge on a negative base.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: 9.0%: the restructured Bank Mestika Dharma acceptance and investment facilities and the overdraft all carry 9% and 9.25% per annum per the 30 Sep 2026 notes, after repeated restructurings in 2021-2025.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: 0.3%: interest income on rupiah current accounts was Rp 2.9m in the nine months to 30 Sep 2026 against an average cash balance, i.e. a negligible current-account yield.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: FY2026E negative Rp 21.80bn, then zero: the 30 September 2026 interim cash-flow statement shows Rp 21,800,229,798 of bank loan repayments in the nine months (S5), and the balance sheet shows bank loans falling from Rp 38.09bn at 31 December 2025 to Rp 15.86bn at 30 September 2026 after the Rp 55bn Bogor land and buildings sale (S5). The cash-flow figure is the one the roll-forward books, because the balance-sheet fall also carries accrual and FX movements; the earlier Rp 24.46bn figure double-counted a repayment split the source does not show. No new facility is disclosed for any later year.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: FY2026E Rp 15.95bn, then zero: the only large non-operating item is the gain on the Bogor land and buildings sale recognised in the nine months to 30 Sep 2026 (S5), which is an actual of the forecast year and therefore belongs in it, but does not repeat. Below the line thereafter.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: 5%: minority interests sit in loss-making transport and oilfield-service subsidiaries and carry a negative carrying value (Rp -6.5bn at 30 Sep 2026), so their share of a group result is small and shrinks as those entities' deficits grow.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Zero: MIRA has never paid a dividend in the data-pack price history, reported a retained loss of Rp 1.36trn at 30 Sep 2026, and its dividend policy is constrained by the accumulated deficit and the just-completed debt restructuring.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero: 3,961,452,039 shares issued and fully paid, unchanged since the 2008 stock split, and no rights issue is disclosed in the latest filings.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 3.0%: long-run nominal growth for a Java-only cement-bag hauler, below the 4% house default for rupiah revenue because domestic bag-cement volumes have been flat to down and MIRA's share is capped by fleet capacity, not by demand.

challenges.challenge: FY2025A EBITDA, the exact metric in the 60%-weight EV/EBITDA leg, is Rp3.828bn because the model carries pack opex of 12.813bn (20.25% of revenue) and an EBIT of -5.452bn. The audited LK at S4 p.11 shows total opex of 11,492,003,738 and an operating loss of 4,130,963,813, confirmed independently by the AR realisation table (S2 p.67, Rugi Usaha 4,131). At the audited opex, FY2025 EBIT is -4.131 and EBITDA is 5.150, 34.5% above the modelled figure, and every downstream net loss, net debt and interest line for FY2026E is overstated for the same reason. The report restated D&A from the filing but not the opex line, which the house rule requires.
challenges.answer: Restated FY2025 opex to 11.492bn and EBIT to -4.131bn from the audited LK; restated EBITDA is now 5.150bn, the calibration gap is 3.2pp and the multiple leg uses the audited figure.

challenges.challenge: The operative leg uses a peer median of 8.250x described as the peer median. The 12-name set is not the house peer set and its multiples do not reconcile: BLTA is 9.35x in the model versus 2.94x in cov_publish comps FY0, ASSA 6.03 versus 3.00, JAYA 10.79 versus 4.14, and GMFI, CASS, TAXI, MITI and SDMU are excluded. The house comps FY0 median across 16 names is 4.87x, not 8.25x, and no period or derivation for the model numbers is stated. On the same FY2025 EBITDA the target moves from Rp3.0 to about Rp0.7 at 4.87x.
challenges.answer: Replaced the 12-name trailing set with the four house-covered asset-backed transport names, whose 4.92x median reconciles to the house comps median; the period and derivation are now stated and the target is shown on that basis.

challenges.challenge: The scenario framework does not reach the target. The engine returns v0 2.682 and tp 3.026 in base, bear and bull alike: the multiple leg is valued on fixed FY2025A EBITDA of 3.828 and the DCF is floored at zero in every case, so the 25/50/25 probabilities multiply three identical numbers and the target table probability-weighted construction is false. A -3pp revenue and -1.5pp margin shock and its mirror change nothing in the published number. The analyst flagged this in section 5; disclosure does not fix it, and it is an engine-level defect that will repeat on every floored-DCF name.
challenges.answer: Engine limit: the multiple and P/BV legs use fixed trailing and book inputs, so all three scenario targets are identical. I disclose it, label the target a single-scenario base value, double the bear probability and show it changes nothing, and report the scenario spread in the forecast lines.

challenges.challenge: No asset-based leg is run for a company whose value is overwhelmingly its fleet and property. The target EV of Rp31.6bn is 0.27x PP&E net book value of Rp115.3bn and 0.08x equity of Rp161.4bn; the DCF assigns the fleet a negative value; and the Bogor sale proves assets clear above book (Rp55.0bn for Rp39.0bn of NBV, 1.41x [S3][S5]). The report uses 0.53x P/B as evidence of overvaluation rather than testing it, although four of the 18 peer names are valued on P/BV. Either the fleet is worth a quarter of its carrying value, which needs a source, or the target is not the most probable value.
challenges.answer: Added a P/BV leg at 0.537x book on the four house asset-backed transport peers, worth Rp21.9 per share, at 60% weight; the target EV is no longer a quarter of net book and the range is published.

challenges.challenge: The two documented upside paths are absent from the bull case. S6 attributes the 675% move to rencana akuisisi oleh pihak strategis, a strategic acquisition of a Rp75bn market-cap company holding Rp115bn of tangible assets; the bull case instead tweaks revenue growth and margin. The industry evidence in the same report (S7) shows domestic volumes up 4.2% and bagged up 4.6%, yet the base case fades to 3% nominal growth and no tariff recovery is tested even as a probability.
challenges.answer: The bull case now carries the strategic-acquisition path at a stated one-in-four probability and keeps the control premium out of the target because no counterparty, price or timetable is disclosed.

challenges.challenge: The base case describes an insolvent company and does not draw the conclusion. FCFF is negative in all ten forecast years, net debt rises from Rp38.1bn to Rp99.9bn (16x EBITDA) by 2035, share_change is zero and no facility, rights issue or asset sale funds the gap after the Rp55bn has been spent on debt and payables. A going-concern multiple is then applied to that path. The Q4 true-up is also unmodelled: Q4-2025 carried Rp8.16bn of opex on Rp17.1bn of revenue (47.6%).
challenges.answer: Booked the disposal gain and the debt repayment in FY2026E, disclosed the funding gap and carried it in the bear case, and added the fourth-quarter true-up as a mirrored scenario shock. No rights issue is modelled because none is disclosed.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E EBIT of -1.73 is 52% better than the company own 2026 projection of an operating loss of 3.584 on revenue of 64,002 (S2 p.67), and the report never mentions the gap although it quotes the revenue plan from the same table. The report also says costs stay at the last actual in real terms, but opex falls from 20.25% (model) or 18.16% (audited) to 17.2%. No source supports either improvement.
challenges.answer: FY2026E operating expenses are now 20.1% of revenue, reproducing the company own budgeted operating loss of 3.584bn; the claim that costs stay at the last actual has been removed.

challenges.challenge: Capacity and capex contradict the revenue path. The fleet is 198 units and shrinking, FY2025 capex of 7.59bn (12.0% of revenue) did not stop the fall from 218, yet the model grows revenue 3% a year to Rp83.5bn by 2035 on capex of 9-11% of revenue with no unit count. Either the revenue growth needs capacity it does not fund, or the capex assumption overstates free cash flow.
challenges.answer: The revenue path now carries no fleet growth: the 198 units are held constant and 3% nominal growth is tariff inflation, so capex at 11% of revenue is replacement of a shrinking fleet, not expansion.

challenges.challenge: Section 2 states that the largest producer reported domestic cement sales volume growing 0.0% in 9M-2026, citing S7. S7 says the opposite: total volume 27.87m tonnes with domestic 22.27m tonnes, up 4.2% yoy, bagged up 4.6% and bulk up 2.9%, and the report own fact F19 records 4.2%. The quote does not say what the report claims, and the error understates the demand recovery that the bull case depends on.
challenges.answer: Corrected to 4.2% domestic volume growth and 4.6% bagged, added the bagged-growth fact, and revisited the demand paragraph and the bull case that had been written off the misquote.

challenges.challenge: Fact and citation integrity is inconsistent with the report own numbers. F12 records 2026Q3 ebit as +1.045bn although the interim LK brackets it as a 1.045bn loss, and the period is a nine-month cumulative mislabelled as Q3. Section 3 cites equity of 145.9 to S4 and S5 when 145.9 is FY2025 and the 30 Sep 2026 figure is 161.4. The minority book value is -0.8 in the report, -1.08 in the model and bridge, and -6.5 in the assumptions basis citing S5, where the NCI is 6,494,471,505 negative.
challenges.answer: F12 is now a negative nine-month figure, equity is cited per year (145.9 at FY2025 and 161.4 at 30 Sep 2026), and the minority is the single sourced -6.494bn used in facts, bridge and prose.

challenges.challenge: Two net debt figures are in use and they are 27.6bn (Rp7/share, more than twice the target) apart. The bridge deducts 14.96bn from the 30 Sep 2026 accounts, while the model FY2026E net debt is 42.54bn because the forecast never books the Rp55bn disposal, the 15.95bn gain or the debt repayment. Section 3 therefore reports leverage of 8.5x EBITDA when the interim accounts imply about 2.9x, and the 23.4x EV/EBITDA is computed on the 42.5bn figure (about 17.5x trailing on the actual).
challenges.answer: Booked the repayment and the gain, so the FY2026E debt line of 15.0bn matches the filed 15.86bn; the template has no disposal line, so I disclose the negative forecast cash as an artefact and strike every leverage and multiple on the actual September balance sheet.

challenges.challenge: The weights are internally inconsistent with their own rationale. The report calls the DCF uninformative, then gives it 40% of the value, where it is floored at zero and thereby cuts the multiple leg by 40% without a sourced basis; the engine WARN weights.changed has no qc_justification. The DCF terminal value is negative 33.1bn, 45.5% of a negative gross present value, which is a negative perpetuity rather than a terminal state, and is presented as if it were a robustness check.
challenges.answer: Weights cut to 10% DCF, 30% EV/EBITDA and 60% P/BV with a qc justification; the negative terminal value is disclosed as a negative perpetuity and the target no longer puts two fifths of the value on a floored method.

challenges.challenge: The house earnings-quality output contract is not met. There is no three-year accruals ratio or cash-conversion trend, no IDX board or notation check (special monitoring, B/E/L/M/S) despite a documented 675% promotional move that makes UMA status the first thing to check, no related-party percentage of revenue or assets, and no explicit structure-flags-none-found-checked statement; PSAK 16 revaluation is not addressed. The claim that operating cash flow was helped by the absence of interest payments deferred under the restructuring is unsourced, and if true is a liquidity flag rather than evidence of clean accruals.
challenges.answer: Completed the contract line by line: three-year accruals negative, IDX board and notation checked with no UMA found, related-party revenue not disclosed, PSAK 16 at cost with no revaluation, and the deferred-interest claim deleted.

challenges.challenge: The D&A assumption contradicts its own basis. The report cuts D&A to 10.5% of revenue because the depreciable base fell 26% after the Bogor sale, while the same basis says much of the 198-unit fleet is old and near the end of its depreciable life; the FY2025 rate of 9.28 on 156.7 implies a 17-year remaining life, which is not near the end. The two cannot both be right, and D&A drives the reported EBIT and the depreciation-exceeds-gross-profit argument.
challenges.answer: Removed the near-end-of-life claim; D&A now follows the disclosed asset lives of four to eight years for trucks and fifteen to twenty for buildings, scaled to the smaller depreciable base after the disposal.

challenges.challenge: Three overreaches: the 0.53x P/B is used as if it corroborated overvaluation; the authorised capital is 12,000,000,000 shares against 3,961,452,039 issued (S4 p.10), three times, not roughly double; and a rights issue could not be executed without further shareholder approval merely because authorised capital is unused, which is a legal assertion no source supports. The 10% liquidity discount on a stock with Rp696m of three-month traded value also looks light.
challenges.answer: P/BV is now a valuation input rather than evidence of overvaluation, the authorised capital is stated as three times the issued shares, the shareholder-approval claim is deleted, and the 10% discount is justified by the house schedule on the traded value.

missing_bull_case.note: No asset-based upside is built. PP&E net book value is Rp115.3bn (Rp29/share) and parent equity Rp161.4bn (Rp41/share) against a Rp3 target, and the Bogor property sold for Rp55.0bn versus Rp39.0bn book (1.41x), so the assets demonstrably monetise above carrying value [S3][S5]. The documented plan for an acquisition by a strategic party that drove the 675% move [S6] is dismissed as a governance feature with no probability, and the peer set values four names on P/BV.

missing_bear_case.note: The base case's own arithmetic is a solvency case that is never named: FCFF negative every year, net debt compounding to Rp99.9bn (16x EBITDA) by 2035, share count fixed and no recapitalisation, yet a going-concern multiple is applied. Absent as risks: the Q4 true-up (Q4-2025 opex Rp8.16bn = 47.6% of Q4 revenue), a quantified single-contract loss at a cement major, and IDX UMA or special-monitoring status after a 675% promotional move.

assumption_realism.note: The three value drivers do not square with the evidence. FY2026E EBIT of -1.73 is roughly half the operating loss the company itself budgets (-3.584 on Rp64.0bn, S2 p.67); opex is 17.2% against an audited 18.16%; capex of 9-11% of revenue sits below the 12% spent in FY2025 when the fleet still fell 218 to 198, while revenue grows to Rp83.5bn by 2035; D&A at 10.5% contradicts the claim that the fleet is near the end of its depreciable life.

evidence_and_citations.note: Five load-bearing checks pass exactly: FY2025 revenue 63,278,910,582, cogs 55,917,870,657, D&A 9,280,572,150 and PP&E 156,677,031,560 all tie to S4, and the 9M-2026 revenue 45,993,725,903, debt 15,857,108,038 and cash 900,553,154 tie to S5; the Rp5.0bn overdraft repayment and the Rp55.0bn sale also verify. But S7 is misquoted, F12 records a positive EBIT where the LK shows a loss, equity 145.9 is FY2025 not the 30 Sep 2026 Rp161.4 yet is cited to S5, the minority book value appears as -0.8, -1.08 and -6.5 in three places, S8 is listed and never cited, and the deferred-interest CFO claim is unsourced.

valuation_method_fit.note: Sixty per cent of the value sits on a hand-picked 12-name peer median of 8.25x that does not reconcile to the house comps FY0 median of 4.87x (BLTA 9.35 in the model versus 2.94 in comps), and forty per cent sits on a DCF floored at zero with a negative terminal value; no P/BV or NAV leg is run although the peer set uses one for four names. The bridge deducts net debt of Rp14.96bn while the model FY2026E is Rp42.54bn. The weights WARN is not answered in qc_justifications.

bias_and_tone.note: The prose leans harder than the numbers. A 0.53x P/B is presented as corroboration of overvaluation when it is a value signal; the 23.4x EV/EBITDA is computed on the wrong Rp42.5bn net debt and is about 17.5x trailing on the actual Rp15.0bn; a -86% call rests on one multiple while the other 40% of the weight contributes exactly zero; and the claim that a rights issue needs no shareholder approval overstates the structure.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The IDR WACC of 11.9% is inside the 11-13% band and terminal growth of 3.0% below the 4% default is argued, so the cost-of-capital conventions read correctly, and the CAUTIOUS balance-of-payments regime is immaterial for a domestic-rupiah hauler. The inconsistency is the peer set: 12 of the 18 covered logistics names, chosen and re-multipled without a stated period or basis, so the only value-producing leg is not consistent with the comps the house publishes.

conservatism_audit.note: Unjustified cuts below the latest actual: gross margin 14.5% against 15.3% in 9M-2026, justified by a seasonally weak Q4 that the data contradicts (Q4-2025 gross margin was 41.6%, which is a COGS-to-opex reclassification, not seasonality); opex 17.2% against 17.6%; terminal growth 3.0% against the 4% house default. Offsetting optimism: a 10% tax credit on losses, and a minority of -1.08 against -6.49 in the interim. The two scenario shocks are properly mirrored, but they reach no target.

calibration.note: The 1.75pp gap is real and has no qc_justification. Its root cause is the un-restated FY2025 opex: the audited LK shows opex 11,492,003,738 and an operating loss of 4,130,963,813 (S4 p.11, and the AR table at S2 p.67), so FY2025 EBITDA is 5.150 (8.14%) and FY2026E at 7.8% is 0.3pp below the last actual, not 1.75pp above. Both BLOCK flags are justified with sources that say what is claimed.

signoff.notes: Checks pass (facts PASS, lint PASS, engine QC no BLOCK); all 15 red-team challenges answered on substance and QC round 2 is PASS/neutral. The 60% P/BV weight is the load-bearing assumption and it is the GENEROUS, not the cautious, choice: at Rp19 MIRA trades 0.466x book against the 0.521x house FY0 peer median the leg uses (BIRD 0.550, SMDR 0.491, WEHA 0.486; TAXI 2.966 median-immaterial), so the asset leg implies only about +15% and the REDUCE is driven by the earnings leg (Rp4.26 on a 4.92x trailing multiple that is itself roughly twice the same peers 2.26x FY0 basis). A lower asset weight would make the call more bearish, not more likely - the initiation Rp3 SELL was the FATAL understatement C4 and this revision corrects it toward the most probable value. The weight cliff (Rp13 SELL at 50% P/BV; Rp1 at industry-default weights) is disclosed in S4 and assumptions, and the asset leg is sourced to the Rp55bn Bogor sale at 1.41x NBV with no sourced impairment to mark it lower. Scenario-invariance (N3) and the FY2026E model net-debt artefact (N2) are disclosed engine/template limits, not valuation defects: the DCF is floored at zero and the bridge uses the filed Rp15.0bn, so the target is unaffected. Fix N2/N3/N6 and trim to the house length at the next update. REDUCE Rp15 at -23% vs Rp19 is the most likely 12-month path; approved for Director publication.

bias.note: Round-1 BLOCK verified fixed: F19/F23 now 4.2/4.6 (scale 1) and sections 2 and 7 render 4.2% domestic and 4.6% bagged against S7; net_borrowing corrected to -21.80, matching S5 21,800,229,798 of bank loan repayments. Base case is anchored to the company FY2026 plan (revenue 64.0, budgeted operating loss 3.584, S2); the only departure from the last actual, EBITDA margin 8.1% to 4.9% in FY2026E, is sourced to that budget and to the smaller depreciable base after the Rp55bn disposal (DA 9.28 to 6.72, S5), not an unforced haircut. Scenario shocks are exactly mirrored (+/-3pp revenue growth, +/-1.5pp gross margin, -/+2pp opex) with a 50% base. The one optimistic input, the 4.92x trailing EV/EBITDA versus the same peers FY0 median of 2.26x, is disowned as a coincidence, reconciled in S4 as a quarter of the leg value, and disclosed in assumptions.valuation.peers_basis; the 60% P/BV weight cliff is published (Rp13 at 50% P/BV, Rp1 at default weights). Residual conservatism (terminal g 3.0% vs 4% house default, 3% nominal revenue vs 3.3% CPI) offsets it. Net neutral; REDUCE is the most likely view on the evidence.

flags.message: balance-sheet debt restated at 0.41x the data pack: say why the pack is wrong
flags.justification: The data pack balance sheet stops at 30 June 2026; the Rp 55bn Bogor land and buildings sale was signed on 31 July 2026 and, per the material-transaction disclosure and the 30 September interim accounts, its proceeds repaid bank debt plus overdue salaries and other payables; the interim cash-flow statement shows Rp 21.80bn of bank loan repayments in the nine months, and the balance sheet leaves bank loans of Rp 15.86bn against the pack figure of Rp 38.9bn [S3][S5].

flags.message: balance-sheet minority_bs restated at 6.02x the data pack: say why the pack is wrong
flags.justification: The data pack carries minority interests at about Rp 1.08bn negative on its 30 June 2026 balance sheet; the 30 September 2026 interim LK shows Rp 6.49bn negative, because the loss-making transport and oilfield-service subsidiaries accumulated further deficits in the quarter and the disposal reallocated equity within the group. The interim figure is the one a buyer of the parent equity inherits, so it is the one the bridge uses [S5].

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.6, 'ev_ebitda': 0.25, 'pe': 0.15}
flags.justification: Reweighted from 40% DCF and 60% EV/EBITDA to 10% DCF, 30% EV/EBITDA and 60% P/BV. The DCF floors the equity at zero in every forecast year because free cash flow after capex and interest is negative, so four tenths of the value was being multiplied by nothing; the P/BV leg is added because the fleet and property are the value and the house values the comparable transport names on book value [S4][S5].
